title: Pipeline Readiness Score
subtitle: Measures how ready your financial services firm is to build a predictable, marketing-driven pipeline that does not depend on introductions.

questions.text: If your three strongest referrers stopped sending work tomorrow, how much of your new business would disappear?

answers.label: More than 80% — it would be a serious crisis
60 to 80% — it would be a very difficult year
40 to 60% — we would notice but we would manage
20 to 40% — we have other sources coming through
Less than 20% — referrals are a bonus, not the engine

questions.text: How does your pipeline typically look in the absence of a warm introduction?

answers.label: We have no real pipeline without introductions
Occasionally a prospect finds us another way, but it is rare
We get some direct enquiries but they are inconsistent
We have a steady trickle of non-referral enquiries
We have predictable inbound from marketing channels

questions.text: When a prospect contacts you without a referral, where do they usually say they found you?

answers.label: This almost never happens
They mention our name through word of mouth but not a direct introduction
Our website — but we do not know how they got there
Our content or social media
We track this and most non-referral enquiries trace back to our content or digital presence

low.headline: Your pipeline is built on borrowed trust
low.text: Right now, your firm's future is largely in someone else's hands. That is not a criticism — financial services firms are built this way more often than not — but it is a real risk. The firms that move past it do not abandon referrals. They build a second engine alongside them.
steps: Audit your last 24 months of new business: name every source and calculate what percentage came from introductions
Identify the two or three questions your ideal clients research before deciding who to call — those are your first content briefs
Set a 12-month target for non-referral enquiries, even a modest one, and track it monthly

mid.headline: You have some inbound — now make it predictable
mid.text: Non-referral enquiries are coming through, which means the groundwork is there. The gap at this stage is usually production: the point of view exists, the discipline exists, but there is no consistent process making it the default rather than something that happens when there is time.
steps: Map your current non-referral enquiry sources and understand what content or touchpoints preceded them
Build a production process — assign ownership, set a cadence, and treat content like client work: scheduled, not squeezed in
Run a six-month test: publish consistently on one channel and measure whether non-referral enquiry volume shifts

high.headline: You are running a real second engine
high.text: You have moved past the point where introductions are your only source of new business. The focus now is on strengthening the non-referral side — improving the fit quality of inbound, extending your reach into new segments, and protecting the consistency that is producing these results.
steps: Compare the fit quality of referral versus non-referral clients: retention rate, fee level, ease of onboarding
Invest in the content and channels that are already producing results rather than spreading attention equally
Document your process so it does not depend on any one person to keep running

questions.text: How often does your firm publish content that addresses the questions your ideal clients are actually asking?

answers.label: We do not publish regularly
We publish occasionally — a few times a year when prompted
We publish monthly but it is inconsistent
We publish on a consistent schedule
We publish consistently and it is tied to what our ideal clients are searching for and asking

questions.text: When a prospect is in their research phase — reading before they decide who to call — how visible is your firm?

answers.label: We are probably not visible at all
We might appear if they search our name, but not the questions they are asking
We have some content out there but it is scattered and not current
We appear in searches for some of the questions our clients ask
We consistently show up during the research phase for our target audience

questions.text: How does content get produced at your firm?

answers.label: One person does it when they have time, which is not often
We have produced content in bursts but it always stalls
We have an informal process but consistency is the hardest part
We have a process and someone owns it, but it is still ad hoc in practice
We have a production process that makes consistency the default, not something that happens when there is time

questions.text: How many hours per week does your team spend on referral relationship management — lunches, events, introductions, and follow-ups?
questions.hint: Include all fee-earning time spent maintaining introducer relationships, not just formal meetings

low.headline: You are invisible during the research phase
low.text: There is a research phase before almost every significant financial services engagement. Someone with a question about their pension, their business sale, or their portfolio will spend real time reading before they decide who to speak to. Right now, your firm is probably not in that conversation.
steps: List the five questions your best clients asked before they first contacted you — those are your first five content briefs
Choose one channel to publish on consistently and commit to a cadence you can actually maintain
Assign a single owner for content production — not a committee, not a shared responsibility

mid.headline: The point of view is there — the production process is not
mid.text: My read: what is usually missing at this stage is not ideas or expertise, it is a production process that makes consistency the default. The firms that build real visibility do not publish more than others. They stop treating content as something that happens when there is time.
steps: Audit your existing content: what has performed, what has prompted enquiries, what is now out of date
Build a quarterly content calendar around the questions your ideal clients research — plan it once, execute consistently
Track which content is driving website visits and ask every non-referral enquiry where they found you

high.headline: You are showing up during the research phase — keep building
high.text: The slow build is real, and then it becomes something different. The firms that invest consistently in content see enquiries arrive where the person has already read through several things and has a clear sense of whether the firm is right for them. The fit tends to be stronger. The client retention tends to be better. You are on that path.
steps: Review whether your content is specific enough to your audience — does it speak to the exact people you want, or to financial services clients broadly
Look at where your best-fit clients found you and invest more in those channels
Build depth where you have breadth: full topic areas rather than isolated articles

questions.text: If your ideal client landed on your website today with no prior knowledge of your firm, how clearly would they understand who you serve and what changes for them?

answers.label: It describes what we do but a first-time visitor would not know if we are right for them
It covers our services clearly but does not speak to a specific audience
It is reasonable — they would understand our offer but might not feel it was written for their situation
It is clear for the right visitor — someone who fits our ideal client profile would see themselves in it
It is specific — a visitor who matches our ideal client would immediately recognise that we understand their world

questions.text: How sector-specific is your firm's marketing and positioning?

answers.label: We position ourselves as financial services generalists
We name our sectors but do not tailor the message to each
We have different pages or sections for each audience but the messaging is similar
We tailor our approach to each sector we work in
Each audience we serve sees messaging, tone, and evidence specific to their world

questions.text: How does your website perform as a trust-building asset before a prospect picks up the phone?

answers.label: Most visitors are probably confirming we exist after a referral — the site is not doing independent work
It looks credible but does not actively build trust
It has some useful content but is not consistently persuasive
It does a reasonable job of establishing credibility for visitors who reach it
It builds genuine trust through content, specificity, and evidence — it works before we do

low.headline: Your website is a brochure, not a pipeline asset
low.text: A website that only works for people who already know you is a missed opportunity. The prospect who finds you during their research phase — with no introduction and no prior contact — needs to see something specific enough to convince them you understand their world. Right now, that is probably not what they are finding.
steps: Read your home page as a first-time visitor who has never heard of your firm and write down what is unclear
Identify the one audience most important to your next phase and rewrite your core messaging for them specifically
Add three to five pieces of content that answer the questions that audience is actually researching

mid.headline: Your digital presence is credible but not converting
mid.text: There is a difference between a website that looks like a serious firm and one that actively builds trust with the right people. What builds trust with a pension trustee committee works differently from what builds trust with an entrepreneur looking for acquisition finance. The expression has to be specific to your actual audience.
steps: Map the trust signals your ideal client needs to see: specific sector experience, relevant evidence, named credentials

Review how sector-specific your messaging is — a financial planning firm talking to HNW individuals approaching retirement and an asset manager talking to institutional investors need completely different approaches
Rebuild your highest-traffic pages around the specific reader, not the general market

high.headline: Your website is earning its place in the pipeline
high.text: A website that builds trust before you do — demonstrating sector understanding, answering the research-phase questions, showing evidence that is specific to the audience — is a real competitive asset in financial services. The firms that get this right see stronger inbound fit and better client retention over time.
steps: Track which pages are driving the highest-quality enquiries and prioritise improving those first
Review whether your messaging stays current as regulatory guidance shifts — a website needs to move when the environment moves
Test with a cold reader once a year: someone who does not know your firm reviews the site and tells you what they understood

questions.text: How does compliance factor into your content production process?

answers.label: Compliance slows everything down to the point where we have largely stopped trying
We produce content but it often gets flagged and we spend more time fixing it than creating it
We are cautious — we avoid topics that might be difficult to get through review
We have a reasonable process but it still creates bottlenecks
We produce content that is useful and survives review without significant rework

questions.text: How often does a compliance flag or revision cycle cause a piece of content to be significantly delayed or abandoned?

answers.label: Often — it is the main reason we do not publish more
Regularly — at least half our content is significantly affected
Occasionally — it is frustrating but we get there eventually
Rarely — we have learned to write for compliance from the start
Almost never — compliance is built into the brief, not bolted on at the end

questions.text: How much of your marketing time is spent on rework — fixing content that did not survive compliance review or did not land with your audience?

answers.label: Most of it — we spend more time fixing than creating
A significant portion — rework is a constant drain
Some — it is frustrating but manageable
A small amount — we catch most issues before they become problems
Almost none — we get it right on the first pass most of the time

low.headline: Compliance is blocking your marketing rather than working with it
low.text: In financial services, a single line of copy carries liability. Compliance teams need to approve every external communication. That is the normal operating condition — and it is why working with people who know what a compliance function will flag before they see it makes a material difference to what you can actually produce and how fast.
steps: Map the last three pieces of content that went through compliance and identify the most common reasons for flags
Build those patterns into your brief before content is written, not into the review after
Consider whether your current content partner or process understands financial services compliance — the knowledge gap is usually where the rework comes from

mid.headline: You are managing compliance — now make it an advantage
mid.text: The firms that get compliance-ready marketing right do not just avoid flags. They know what will work before they write it, which means they publish more and faster than firms that treat compliance as a final hurdle. That institutional knowledge is a real competitive edge — it changes the speed and quality of what you can deliver.
steps: Document the compliance patterns that consistently delay content and build them into your editorial standards
Make sure whoever writes your content — internal or external — understands the specific requirements of your regulatory environment
Measure the average time from brief to publication and track whether it shortens as compliance becomes part of the process rather than the end of it

high.headline: Compliance is built in, not bolted on
high.text: This is where most financial services firms do not get to. Producing content that is genuinely useful and survives review — consistently, without significant rework — requires people who understand the environment from the inside. You have built that. The priority now is protecting it.
steps: Review your process annually as regulatory guidance shifts — what works today may need updating when the environment moves
Document your compliance-ready brief template so it does not live only in one person's head
Use your compliance knowledge as a filter when evaluating external partners — it is a higher bar than most generalists can meet

questions.text: How well do you understand where your best clients came from before they contacted you?

answers.label: We do not really know — most arrived through introductions and we have not tracked it further
We have a rough sense but no real data
We track referral sources but not what else may have influenced non-referral enquiries
We track sources and have some data on what touched non-referral enquiries before they called
We know exactly what influenced our best clients before they called and we invest in those channels

questions.text: What percentage of your new clients in the last 12 months came through marketing or digital channels — not referrals or introductions?
questions.hint: Include any client who found you through your website, content, social media, or search without a prior introduction

questions.text: What is the average loaded hourly cost of your team's time — salary, employer costs, and overhead divided by working hours? Use your best estimate.
questions.hint: A reasonable starting point for most advisory firms is £75 to £150 per hour

low.headline: You are flying blind on pipeline sources
low.text: If you do not know what influenced your best clients before they called, you cannot invest intelligently in building more of them. This gap is common across financial services firms — and it is one of the main reasons referral dependency persists even when firms want to change it.
steps: Start asking every new client the same two questions: how did you find us, and what did you read or look at before you called
Add a simple source field to your CRM or client intake process and record it for every new enquiry
Estimate what percentage of your last 12 months of new business came from introductions versus other sources — even a rough number is more useful than none

mid.headline: You have some data — now use it to direct investment
mid.text: Knowing where your clients come from is the start. The firms that use that data well are directing their marketing budget and time toward the channels that are already working — not spreading it equally or defaulting to whatever feels most visible.
steps: Build a simple monthly report: new enquiries, source, conversion rate, and average deal or retainer value by source
Compare the fit quality of referral and non-referral clients over the last two years — retention, fee level, ease of working relationship
Set a specific target for non-referral enquiries and review it quarterly

high.headline: You know what is working — keep that measurement discipline
high.text: The firms that move decisively past referral dependency are the ones that track both what is producing pipeline and the quality of what it produces. You are doing this. The question worth asking now is whether you are investing in the right channels in proportion to what they are actually delivering.
steps: Review whether your measurement is capturing the full research trail, not just the last touchpoint before enquiry
Model what a 10-percentage-point shift from referral to marketing-driven would mean for revenue and dependency risk
Use your data when briefing external partners — it is more useful than assumptions about what should work

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: In 30 minutes I'll show you which two gaps to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing.
